heading: 2. H1 is not supported — DNA and RNA functional pools respond comparably to warming

text: The paired n=25 analysis appeared to favor DNA (pseudo-F 3.12, R²=11.9%, p=0.020) over RNA (pseudo-F 0.76, R²=3.2%, p=0.60), but organic samples were all incubated and mineral samples all direct, confounding horizon with incubation; H1 was not supported.
quote: The originally proposed H1 (RNA composition shifts more than DNA under warming) is **not supported** once a horizon × incubation confound is removed. In the paired n=25 subset (samples with both DNA and RNA), PERMANOVA pseudo-F for treatment was 3.12 in DNA (R²=11.9%, p=0.020) vs 0.76 in RNA (R²=3.2%, p=0.60), seemingly contradicting H1 in the opposite direction. However, the paired subset confounds horizon with incubation (every organic sample is incubated, every mineral sample is direct).
heading: 2. H1 is not supported — DNA and RNA functional pools respond comparably to warming

text: Direct-sample sensitivity analyses yielded treatment R²=12.7% in mineral DNA (n=14, F=1.75, p=0.081), 11.4% in mineral RNA (n=11, F=1.15, p=0.254), and 10.0% in organic RNA (n=14, F=1.33, p=0.190).
quote:
**Sensitivity analysis using direct samples only** (no incubation confound):

| Pool × Horizon | n | F | R² | p |
|----------------|----|---|------|------|
| DNA × mineral | 14 | 1.75 | 12.7% | 0.081 |
| RNA × mineral | 11 | 1.15 | 11.4% | 0.254 |
| RNA × organic | 14 | 1.33 | 10.0% | 0.190 |
heading: 2. H1 is not supported — DNA and RNA functional pools respond comparably to warming

text: After removing incubation confounding, DNA and RNA treatment R² were comparable at 10-13%; greater transcript-pool sensitivity was not supported.
quote: DNA and RNA pools show **comparable** treatment R² (10-13%). H1's premise that the transcript pool is more sensitive is not supported in this dataset.
heading: 2. H1 is not supported — DNA and RNA functional pools respond comparably to warming

text: The report proposes, rather than demonstrates, long-term compositional turnover as a possible reason DNA and RNA warming sensitivities converge after roughly 25 years of heating.
quote: 1. **Compositional turnover has caught up.** H1 is grounded in the assumption that regulatory response (transcript-level) precedes community turnover (genome-content). That asymmetry is plausible on weeks-to-years timescales but the Barre Woods plots have been heated since ~1991; 25 years is more than enough time for the genome content to fully reflect warming-selected lineages. DeAngelis et al. (2015) and Pold et al. (2016) document strong genome-content shifts at this site over the same period. Once the DNA-level community has equilibrated, the RNA / DNA ratio of warming sensitivity collapses toward 1.
heading: 2. H1 is not supported — DNA and RNA functional pools respond comparably to warming

text: The single collection date, 2017-05-24, may leave RNA subject to diurnal and microspatial variation, weakening its signal of chronic +5°C warming.
quote: 2. **Single-timepoint RNA carries diurnal and microspatial noise.** All samples were collected on a single date (2017-05-24). Transcript abundances respond to short-timescale conditions (moisture pulses, root exudate availability, diurnal temperature) that are not warming-related. The DNA pool integrates over years and is therefore a cleaner readout of the chronic +5°C signal in this design.
heading: 2. H1 is not supported — DNA and RNA functional pools respond comparably to warming

text: The metatranscriptome recovered 14,302 distinct KOs versus 12,863 in the metagenome; the report proposes that this richer repertoire could dilute treatment signals under relative-abundance analysis.
quote: 3. **Compositional dilution in the transcript pool.** The metatranscriptome assembly recovered 14,302 distinct KOs vs 12,863 in the metagenome (Section "Why RNA more KOs than DNA" in NB02 commit message). The richer rare-organism functional repertoire in RNA increases per-KO variance under a relative-abundance framework and reduces statistical power for detecting treatment-level shifts in any single category.
heading: 2. H1 is not supported — DNA and RNA functional pools respond comparably to warming

text: Substrate depletion and global transcript down-regulation are offered as hypothetical explanations, not measured mechanisms, for the absence of a dominant RNA treatment axis.
quote: 4. **Substrate depletion (Domeignoz-Horta et al. 2022) feeds back to RNA.** If chronic warming has reduced substrate quantity and quality, the active transcriptome may be down-shifted across many functional categories rather than redistributed. Such a "global down-regulation" pattern would produce no preferred axis of treatment-driven variance in the RNA pool, even as the underlying community continues to diverge.
heading: 2. H1 is not supported — DNA and RNA functional pools respond comparably to warming

text: Comparable DNA/RNA R² after multi-decadal warming does not exclude an earlier transient during which RNA leads DNA.
quote: The clean comparable-R² verdict here therefore does not rule out an early transient where RNA leads DNA — it argues that on multi-decadal timescales, the two pools' warming responses converge in magnitude.
heading: 2. H1 is not supported — DNA and RNA functional pools respond comparably to warming

heading: Sample design

text: The design has 42 biosamples, DNA n=28 and RNA n=39 across treatment, horizon and incubation. No metagenomes were produced for organic-direct or some mineral-direct samples, leaving unbalanced coverage and an H1 sensitivity caveat.
quote: 42 biosamples in a factorial design: treatment (control vs heated) × horizon (organic vs mineral) × incubation (direct vs lab-incubated). DNA cohort n=28 (mineral direct + organic incubated), RNA cohort n=39 (full mineral direct + organic direct + organic incubated). Coverage is unbalanced because the underlying NMDC pipeline did not produce metagenomes from organic-direct or some mineral-direct samples — this drives the H1 sensitivity caveat in Finding 2.
heading: Sample design

text: The report states that its organic-horizon Actinobacteria-up/Acidobacteria-down q=0.049 result reproduces DeAngelis et al. 2015. It also cites Pold et al. 2016 for an increased fraction of carbohydrate-degrading genes affiliated with Actinobacteria under warming.
quote: **Site-specific compositional findings (DeAngelis et al. 2015; Pold et al. 2016, 2015):** Our q=0.049 Actinobacteria-up / Acidobacteria-down signal in organic horizon directly reproduces the 16S-amplicon and metagenome-based warming signature reported by the same Harvard Forest research team. DeAngelis et al. (2015, Front. Microbiol.) report Actinobacteria, Alphaproteobacteria, and Acidobacteria as the phyla showing the strongest warming responses across 5/8/20-year warmed plots, with shifts most pronounced in the organic horizon — exactly what we see. Pold et al. (2016, AEM) further show that warming increases the fraction of carbohydrate-degrading genes affiliated with Actinobacteria — a mechanistic complement to our compositional finding.
heading: Literature context

text: The report links reduced heated-mineral ChEBI richness qualitatively to prior soil-carbon loss and substrate-depletion literature. It cites Melillo et al. 2017 for a four-phase oscillating trajectory under +5°C warming and Domeignoz-Horta et al. 2022 for reduced substrate quantity and quality, rather than thermal acclimation, in 28-year warmed plots.
quote: **Long-term carbon loss (Melillo et al. 2017; Domeignoz-Horta et al. 2022):** Our heated-mineral metabolite-richness drop (155 vs 167 ChEBI, p=0.012) is qualitatively consistent with the substrate-depletion narrative emerging from these studies. Melillo et al. (2017, Science) document a 4-phase oscillating soil-C loss trajectory under +5°C warming. Domeignoz-Horta et al. (2022, GCB) — the closest temporal analog (28-year warmed plots) — argue that the apparent warming response is driven by **reduced substrate quantity and quality**, not thermal acclimation. Our reduced metabolite-richness finding is the direct molecular signature this substrate-depletion model predicts.
heading: Literature context

text: Roy Chowdhury et al. 2021 reportedly found a larger treatment effect on KEGG transcripts than CAZymes and ~68% of differentially expressed CAZyme transcripts up in heated soils. The report notes tension with its comparable DNA/RNA R², while cautioning that timepoint, replication and pipeline differ.
quote: **Metatranscriptome at the same site (Roy Chowdhury et al. 2021):** This is the closest published methodological precedent — Harvard Forest metatranscriptomes (organic + mineral horizon, heated vs control). They report that **treatment had a larger effect on KEGG transcripts than on CAZymes**; ~68% of differentially expressed CAZyme transcripts were upregulated in heated soils. Our finding that DNA and RNA respond comparably (10-13% R²) is in tension with their report of larger transcript-level effect, but the comparison is complicated by their different sampling timepoint, replication, and analytical pipeline. Worth noting: their CAZyme up-direction is consistent with our chitinase up-result.
heading: Literature context

text: Choudoir et al. 2025 reportedly found heated-plot isolate pangenomes enriched in central carbohydrate and nitrogen metabolism and reduced codon-usage bias; the report offers this as context for possible within-clade selection.
quote: **Pangenome-level adaptation (Choudoir et al. 2025, mSphere):** Pangenomes of Harvard Forest isolates show heated-plot genomes are enriched in central carbohydrate and N metabolism and show reduced codon usage bias — relevant to interpreting our DNA-level Actinobacteria enrichment as not just a compositional shift but a sub-clade selection.
heading: Literature context

text: Zhang et al. 2024 reportedly observed a 12-61% increase in net CH₄ uptake across depths and more high-affinity USCα methanotrophs at 0-10 cm in subtropical +4°C warming experiments. Applying this mechanism to Harvard Forest is interpretive, not a direct flux measurement there.
quote: **Methanotrophy as a forest-warming response (Zhang et al. 2024):** Our pmoA/pmoB upregulation in both horizons is unexpected for an aerated temperate forest but published in subtropical forest +4°C warming experiments, where net CH₄ uptake increased 12-61% across soil depths and the relative abundance of high-affinity USCα methanotrophs rose at 0-10 cm. This supports the interpretation that warming-induced moisture decrease (a known concomitant of soil warming) increases CH₄ availability for methanotrophs.
heading: Literature context

text: Aliyu et al. 2016 is cited as precedent for coordinated icl/aceA and aceB/glcB upregulation under stress or C2-substrate use in Actinobacteria; this is mechanistic context, not proof of the Harvard Forest mechanism.
quote: **Glyoxylate cycle activation under stress (Aliyu et al. 2016):** Coordinated icl/aceA + aceB/glcB upregulation is a published signature of stress / C2-substrate-utilization in Actinobacteria. The fact that we see this in the heated-mineral RNA pool, in a Harvard Forest soil where Actinobacteria are enriched (Pold et al. 2016 + our data), is mechanistically self-consistent.
heading: Literature context

text: The authors claim novelty for the paired DNA/RNA variance comparison and the local methanotrophy-plus-glyoxylate RNA pattern, while acknowledging precedents elsewhere.
quote: To our knowledge, this is the **first explicit comparison of DNA-pool and RNA-pool warming response variance** in a paired-sample design at Harvard Forest, including the H1 sensitivity check that demonstrates the apparent DNA-vs-RNA imbalance is largely a horizon × incubation artifact. The methanotrophy-up + glyoxylate-up RNA signature is a previously unreported gene-level pattern at this specific site, although both signatures have published precedents elsewhere.
heading: Novel contribution
